claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy composed primarily of Cu and Ni with trace Pt/Pd.
Introducing atomically dispersed, anchored Pt sites will enhance low-temperature CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Introducing atomically dispersed, anchored Pt sites will improve resistance to H2O poisoning.
Introducing atomically dispersed, anchored Pt sites will improve resistance to NO poisoning.
The intervention will improve catalyst lifetime durability.
The intervention can be implemented without increasing the overall Pt content.
Single-atom deposition or reducing-atmosphere annealing can produce isolated Pt atoms in the proposed automotive alloy.
Alloy-composition modifications can create anchoring sites that stabilize isolated Pt atoms against agglomeration.
The intervention will yield uniformly dispersed, anchored single-atom Pt sites integrated into an HEA matrix.
Isolated Pt atoms lower the activation energy for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Isolated Pt atoms facilitate oxygen activation.
The local high-entropy environment around isolated Pt can reduce poisoning by promoting removal of adsorbed CO.
The proposed Pt sites will weaken adsorption by the relevant automotive poisons H2O and NO.
Engineered anchoring sites will retain atomic Pt dispersion during transient operation and aging by preventing agglomeration.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the intervention will lower the oxidation ignition temperature.
The predicted improvements will apply below 150 °C during transient cycling with concurrent H2O and NO exposure.
The catalyst will sustain its performance during accelerated durability testing intended to mimic vehicle-lifetime aging.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises no increase in overall Pt content, but one proposed implementation is single-atom Pt deposition, which would ordinarily add Pt unless an offsetting removal or redistribution strategy is specified.
